enrichment.short_title: Reckitt IP threats counterclaim: strike-out refused
key_facts: Reckitt Benkiser sued Home Pairfum and others for trade mark, design and passing-off infringement over competing air freshener products.
The defendants counterclaimed for unjustified threats and sought to join Reckitt's solicitors Laytons as Part 20 defendants.
Reckitt applied to strike out the threats counterclaim under CPR 3.4 and 3.1, arguing the legislation conflicted with pre-action settlement policy.
Strong pre-litigation threat letters were sent about seven weeks before proceedings; damages and injunctive relief were likely to be modest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications on a trade mark and design infringement claim: strike out of threats counterclaim and joinder of solicitors.
enrichment.outcome: Reckitt's strike-out application dismissed; defendants' application to join Laytons as Part 20 defendants refused.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a statutory threats counterclaim appears low value and largely overlaps main issues, it is not an abuse of process warranting strike out under the CPR; however, a Part 20 joinder pursued mainly to discomfort the claimant's solicitors may properly be refused as disproportionate case management.
legal_issues: Whether CPR powers can strike out a valid statutory threats claim
Tension between IP threats legislation and pre-action protocols
Whether solicitors who sent threatening letters should be joined
When joinder of a client's lawyers is mischievous or illegitimate

enrichment.short_title: Steamship Mutual pre-action disclosure application refused
key_facts: Steamship Mutual trustees claimed BAM under-performed a US$210m portfolio by about $32m against benchmark in 2000-2001.
After termination of BAM's mandate, the applicants sought internal risk-control and tracking-error documents before deciding whether to sue.
BAM had already provided substantial voluntary disclosure and argued the Professional Negligence Pre-Action Protocol made the application premature.
The application alone cost the parties about £150,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for pre-action disclosure under section 33(2) of the Supreme Court Act 1981 and CPR Part 31.16.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; although some jurisdictional thresholds were met, discretion was exercised against ordering pre-proceedings disclosure.
enrichment.ratio: Where broad negligence issues are identifiable, sufficient voluntary disclosure has been given, no Letter of Claim has been served under the protocol, and further documents would not materially assist the decision to litigate, the court should refuse CPR 31.16 disclosure as disproportionate satellite litigation.

Interaction with the Professional Negligence Pre-Action Protocol

enrichment.short_title: Barnet FC Underhill sale: rectification claim fails
key_facts: Barnet sold the Underhill football ground freehold to Barnet Football Club Holdings for £10,000 with restrictive covenants and an overage deed.
The overage deed allowed further consideration if covenants were varied within a ten-year cut-off period; Barnet claimed it mistakenly believed there was no time limit.
Barnet sought rectification of the transfer and supplemental deed on unilateral mistake and sharp-practice grounds.
Barnet also argued the disposal required consent under section 123(2) but Holdings relied on section 128(2) validation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for rectification of sale documents and related challenge to a local authority land disposal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; rectification refused and the section 123 challenge was barred by section 128(2).
enrichment.ratio: Where the council's authorised decision document expressly contemplated a ten-year overage cut-off, rectification cannot re-write the bargain on unilateral mistake; a disponee claiming under the authority is protected by section 128(2) even when the council itself seeks to recover the land.
legal_issues: Unilateral mistake and unconscionable conduct in rectification
Construction of overage and restrictive covenant arrangements
Whether disposal consent was required under section 123(2)
Protection of disponees under section 128(2)

enrichment.short_title: TUPE transfer of part of building maintenance undertaking

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: Botes held Southwark's borough-wide Major Voids building maintenance contract from 1996 to April 1999.
On re-tendering the borough was split into Area 1 and Area 2; Fairhurst won Area 2 but refused to take on Botes employees.
Nine employees claimed unfair dismissal; the employment tribunal held there was a TUPE transfer of part of the undertaking to Area 2.
Mr Salih was on sick leave and the tribunals disagreed whether he was employed in the transferred part immediately before the transfer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on TUPE applicability and employee inclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Fairhurst's appeal dismissed; Salih cross-appeal dismissed with remittal on whether he was employed in Area 2 immediately before transfer.
enrichment.ratio: A part transferred under TUPE need not have existed as a discrete economic entity before partition if it can be carved out of a larger stable entity and retains its identity after transfer; sickness absence does not of itself exclude an employee from the transferred part.
legal_issues: Whether Area 2 existed as an economic entity before transfer
Meaning of transfer of part of an undertaking under regulation 3
Whether an employee on sick leave was employed in the transferred part
Application of Allen v ACC and Hassard v McGrath

enrichment.short_title: Wrongful conviction compensation permission applications refused
key_facts: Three claimants sought permission to review the Home Secretary's refusal of ex-gratia compensation after their convictions were quashed.
Compensation falls under Mr Hurd's 1985 scheme: serious default by police or public authorities, or complete exoneration in exceptional circumstances.
Issues included whether a judge is a public authority under limb 1 and whether judicial error can be exceptional under limb 2.
Claims concerned export offence misdirection, Polly Peck handling misdirection, and Asil Nadir bail ruling error.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for permission to apply for judicial review of ex-gratia compensation refusals, heard together with oral permission for the third claimant.
enrichment.outcome: All three permission applications failed; challenges on public authority, sentence length, judicial misconduct, and prosecuting counsel conduct held unarguable.
enrichment.ratio: A judge is not a public authority for limb 1 of the 1985 scheme; mere judicial misdirection or sentencing error quashing a conviction does not ordinarily constitute exceptional circumstances under limb 2, and the Secretary of State's evaluative refusals were not irrational.
legal_issues: Whether a judge is a public authority under the 1985 ex-gratia scheme
Whether judicial error can amount to exceptional circumstances
Whether sentence length can itself be exceptional
Rationality of refusal where Court of Appeal quashed convictions

enrichment.short_title: Foster unfair dismissal: EAT could not cut contributory fault
key_facts: Mrs Foster, an administrative assistant in Somerset County Council's fire brigade, was dismissed after a protracted breakdown in workplace relations.
The employment tribunal found substantive fairness but held procedural defects would not have mattered and assessed 100% contributory fault.
The EAT held dismissal procedurally unfair and reduced contributory fault from 100% to 90%.
Both sides appealed: the council on EAT jurisdiction over contributory fault and Mrs Foster on remittal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on unfair dismissal and contributory fault.
enrichment.outcome: Council's appeal allowed; tribunal decision restored; cross-appeal dismissed with costs of appeal limited to £2,500.
enrichment.ratio: A finding of contributory fault is a finding of fact which the EAT may interfere with only if perverse; finding procedural unfairness does not permit the EAT to substitute its own causation finding where the tribunal held the employee would still have been dismissed.
legal_issues: Scope of appeal permitted by EAT rule 3.10
Whether EAT had jurisdiction to alter contributory fault not appealed
Distinction between procedural unfairness and contributory conduct
Whether remittal for rehearing was required

enrichment.short_title: Lydiate conspiracy conviction and sentence appeals refused

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: After a three-month trial Lydiate was convicted by 10-2 majorities of conspiracy to murder and to kidnap and falsely imprison following a Salford shooting.
The prosecution case was a revenge campaign to locate and kill those believed responsible, involving torture of Foster, Kent and Shenton at Hickey Farm.
Foster identified Lydiate at the farm without an identification parade; phone evidence linked Lydiate to Shawcross and co-accused.
Lydiate received life with a 15-year tariff notionally and concurrent 22-year sentences on the other counts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction and sentence after refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Leave refused on both conviction and sentence; fresh evidence from Rowles not admitted under section 23.
enrichment.ratio: Identification evidence admissible as pure recognition without a parade where fairness is not undermined; a sentencer may take account of brutal means used to execute conspiracies without separate substantive counts; 22 years was not manifestly excessive for the totality.
legal_issues: Admissibility of identification evidence without Code D parade after Forbes
Section 34 adverse inference from silence about Shawcross tip
Whether inadmissible hearsay about Lydiate required jury discharge

enrichment.short_title: I-Way screaming.net ISP contract liability judgment
key_facts: I-Way agreed to provide internet access platform services to Localtel's screaming.net free off-peak ISP venture from April 1999.
Localtel projected user uptake and a 20:40:40 call profile; actual daytime use was about 13%, straining I-Way's economics.
At a 14 May 1999 meeting the parties agreed I-Way would retain 30% rather than 20% of telco rebates; Localtel later claimed only a temporary accrual arrangement.
About 20 months later Localtel diverted customers to its own server and invoiced over £700,000 for the withheld 10% share.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Liability trial on misrepresentation, contractual variation, repudiatory breach and exclusivity in an ISP supply agreement.
enrichment.outcome: I-Way succeeded: 70/30 rebate variation upheld as compromise, no repudiatory breach, and customer diversion breached implied exclusivity.
enrichment.ratio: Contemporary correspondence and conduct showed a permanent 70/30 rebate variation compromising misrepresentation claims; where users registering via Localtel CDs were contractually tied to I-Way's server, deliberate migration to a rival platform breached the agreement.
legal_issues: Whether pre-contract projections were actionable misrepresentations
Effect of the 14 May 1999 rebate variation and alleged forged 18 May letter
Whether refusal to pay accrued 10% was repudiatory
Implied term preventing diversion of registered users to another server

key_facts: A 1997 ferroalloy supply agreement between Faronly and Zestafoni contained a three-arbitrator London arbitration clause.
Ronly and Zestafoni Plant ad hoc agreed to appoint Ian Kinnell QC as sole arbitrator over debts exceeding US$17m.
Zestafoni Plant later challenged jurisdiction, title to sue, and alleged Georgian law invalidity of the ad hoc agreement.
The arbitrator held he had jurisdiction and that Ronly could sue in its own name under clause 19.

enrichment.outcome: Section 67 application dismissed; leave to appeal under section 69 refused.

enrichment.short_title: Mesothelioma costs estimate not a costs cap
key_facts: Leslie Burns died of mesothelioma after asbestos exposure with two employers; quantum was agreed at £175,000 at trial.
Elias J apportioned liability 7/8 to the first defendant and 1/8 to the second defendant.
Claimants' solicitors estimated £35,000 base costs at allocation but the bill exceeded £71,000 excluding success fee.
Defendants argued the estimate capped recoverable costs and that failure to serve the estimate on clients breached the indemnity principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment preliminary issue on whether CPR costs estimates limit recoverable costs.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants' argument failed following Leigh v Michelin; costs estimate does not cap assessment and the remainder of the assessment was adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: A costs estimate under CPR PD 43 para 6.4 is not a costs cap; it may be taken into account only where there is a substantial unexplained divergence, reliance by the paying party, or different case management directions would likely have been made.
legal_issues: Whether allocation questionnaire estimates limit recoverable costs
Effect of failure to serve estimates on clients
Application of Leigh v Michelin Tyre Plc
Whether Fairchild litigation changes justified doubling costs
